e.etymology: A short form of Eleanor, by way of Leonore and Leonora. Eleanor comes from the Occitan name Alienor, whose meaning is uncertain. Edgar Allan Poe used Lenore for the lost love in The Raven.
namesakes: Lenore (the lost love mourned in Edgar Allan Poe's The Raven)

assoc.t: Lenore, the lost love in Poe's poem The Raven

e.etymology: An elaborated form of Adela, the Latinate version of French Adèle, from Germanic adal, noble. It peaked in the United States in the 1880s.
From Sanskrit jaya, victory. It stands alone as a woman's name and forms part of many compound Indian names for both sexes.
In American use a short form of Elaina, a spelling of Elaine, the old French form of Helen. A separate Laina is a Finnish name proposed in the 1800s.
A respelling of Mason, an English occupational surname for a stoneworker, from Old French masson.
A pet name, used in Spanish for Socorro and elsewhere as a playful nickname. It is best known from the French designer Gabrielle Chanel, who was called Coco.

assoc.t: Coco, Pixar's 2017 Day of the Dead film
sounds like cocoa, the chocolate drink

e.note: In Spanish coco means coconut and El Coco is the bogeyman; in Portuguese cocô is a child's word for poop.

e.etymology: A pet form of Golda, the Yiddish name from gold, and a spelling of the English nickname Goldie. Today it is used mainly in Orthodox Jewish families.

assoc.t: Goldy Gopher, University of Minnesota mascot

e.etymology: The Spanish pet form of Manuel, from Hebrew Immanuel, God is with us.
namesakes: Manolo Blahnik (Spanish designer of luxury shoes)

assoc.t: Manolo Blahnik luxury shoes, known as Manolos

e.etymology: An American shortening of Marlene, first used in the 1930s. Marlene is a German blend of Maria and Magdalene, made famous by Marlene Dietrich.
namesakes: Marla Maples (actress, second wife of Donald Trump)
Marla Singer (Helena Bonham Carter's character in Fight Club)
Marla Gibbs (actress on The Jeffersons and 227)

e.etymology: A modern American name, one of a group with Aiyana, Ayanna and Iyanna that rose in the 1990s. Its source is not established.
The Spanish word for rain, from Latin pluvia, used as a given name mainly in Mexico.
e.note: Many English speakers do not know that Spanish ll sounds like y, so expect LOO-vee-uh.

e.etymology: A Spanish compound of María and José, the names of Mary and Joseph, the parents of Jesus. In Spanish it is written María José; US birth records run the two together.
A modern American compound of Mia and Bella, which also reads as the Italian phrase mia bella, my beautiful one.
A modern American compound of Mae and Lee, also written Maylee. Mae is a spelling of May, the month name and an old pet form of Mary and Margaret.
A spelling of Violet, the flower name, from Old French violette, a diminutive of Latin viola. The double t follows Scarlett and the French form Violette.
The name of King Théoden of Rohan in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, taken from Old English theoden, king or lord of a people. Parents also use it as a longer form of Theo.
namesakes: Théoden (King of Rohan in The Lord of the Rings)

assoc.t: King Théoden of Rohan in The Lord of the Rings

e.etymology: The Dutch form of French Romée, from Late Latin Romaeus, a pilgrim to Rome. American parents also use it as a spelling of Romy, the German pet form of Rosemarie.
From the Roman family name Cornelius, thought to come from Latin cornu, horn. In the Book of Acts, the centurion Cornelius is the first Gentile convert to Christianity.
namesakes: Cornelius Vanderbilt (19th-century railroad and shipping tycoon)
Cornelius Fudge (Minister of Magic in Harry Potter)

assoc.t: Cornelius, the chimpanzee scientist of Planet of the Apes

e.note: The short form Corny invites teasing.

e.etymology: A spelling of Italian Giovanni used mainly in Spanish-speaking families. Giovanni is the Italian form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
A one-d spelling of Freddy, the pet form of Frederick, from Germanic frid, 'peace', and ric, 'ruler'. This spelling is most common in Latin American families.

assoc.t: Freddy Krueger, A Nightmare on Elm Street villain
Freddy Fazbear of Five Nights at Freddy's

e.etymology: From the English surname Atlee or Attlee, Middle English atte lee, 'at the meadow or clearing', for someone who lived by one. As a first name it is mostly American and recent.
The Italian word for love, from Latin amor. American parents took it up as a given name in recent decades, alongside Amor and Amora.

assoc.t: That's Amore, Dean Martin's 1953 hit song

e.etymology: From Arabic janna, 'garden', the word for paradise in Islam, which reached South Asia through Persian as jannat. It is a popular girls' name among Urdu, Bengali and Punjabi speakers.
An American respelling of Jolie, the French word for pretty, which English speakers adopted as a given name in the 20th century.

assoc.t: Angelina Jolie, actress (her surname is spelled Jolie)

e.etymology: A respelling of Kyler, an American name of the 1980s and 1990s that blends Kyle with the -er of Tyler. It also matches a rare surname, an anglicized form of Dutch Cuyler.
From Greek aner, 'man', and medesthai, 'to be mindful of, to rule'. In myth Andromeda is the princess chained to a rock and rescued by Perseus; a constellation and a galaxy carry her name.

assoc.t: the Andromeda Galaxy, nearest large galaxy to our own
Greek myth princess rescued by Perseus
The Andromeda Strain, Michael Crichton novel and film

e.etymology: In Punjabi a form of Arjun, from Sanskrit arjuna, 'bright, white', honored among Sikhs through Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru. Separately it is a Dutch short form of Adrianus and an Albanian name.
From Greek Astraia, 'starry', from aster, 'star'. Astraea was the goddess of justice, the last immortal to leave the earth, and was set in the sky as the constellation Virgo.

assoc.t: Greek goddess of justice, set in the sky as Virgo

e.etymology: A phonetic respelling of Crew, which is both an English surname from the town of Crewe and the everyday word for a team. Kru took off as a boys' name in the 2020s.

assoc.t: kru, the title for a Muay Thai teacher

e.meaning: son of Madoc, the fortunate one
e.etymology: A respelling of Maddox, the Welsh surname meaning son of Madoc, an old personal name from Welsh mad, 'fortunate, good'.
A recent American name in the style of Alaya, Malaya and Kalea. The same spelling is used for a Thai girls' name.
A modern elaboration of Eva or a feminine form of Evan with the -ana ending; it is also used as a spelling of Ivana.
